body:
Almost every rechargeable vape uses a lithium-ion battery, the same type that powers phones, laptops and power banks. These batteries are reliable when they are treated well and can fail badly when they are damaged, overheated or misused, which is why a few simple habits matter so much. This guide explains how to use the right charger, why not to leave a device charging unattended, how heat and cold affect batteries, how to recognize a damaged device, how to carry devices without risk of a short circuit, what is different about replaceable batteries, how to build good charging habits and when to stop using a device altogether. It is general information for adults aged 21 and over, not a substitute for the manufacturer's instructions. Nicotine is addictive.

## How a lithium-ion battery works, briefly
A lithium-ion battery stores energy by moving lithium ions between two electrodes. It is compact and powerful, which is why it suits small devices. But it also holds a lot of energy in a small space, and if the internal parts are damaged or the battery is overheated or overcharged, that energy can be released quickly as heat, which is the source of the rare but serious battery fires that make the news. Good habits keep the battery in the range where it behaves as designed.

## Use the right charger
Charge with the cable supplied or a reputable one, from a standard USB port or wall adapter. Cheap, unbranded chargers can supply inconsistent power and may lack the protections that quality chargers include. If your device has a USB-C port, use a good USB-C cable, and avoid frayed or bent connectors. If a cable or a port is damaged, replace it. Do not use a charger with a much higher power rating than the device expects unless the manufacturer says it is supported. See [how to charge a disposable](/blog/how-to-charge-a-disposable/).

## Do not leave it charging unattended
Charge on a hard, flat, non-flammable surface, such as a table or a countertop, and avoid sleeping with a charging device by your bed or on soft furnishings. Do not charge under a pillow, on a sofa or in a bag. Stay in the room while it charges, and unplug it when it is full. A device that charges overnight every night is exposed to more risk than one that charges in daylight under your eye.

## Avoid heat and cold
Do not leave a vape in a hot car or direct sun, and avoid freezing temperatures. Heat shortens battery life and can damage the device. Cold reduces performance temporarily and can harm a battery if you charge it while it is very cold. Let a device return to room temperature before you charge or use it. Keep devices away from radiators, heaters and sunny windowsills. If a device feels hot while charging or using, stop and unplug it.

## Do not use a damaged device
Stop using any device that is swollen, dented, hot to touch, leaking or has damaged wiring. A swollen casing can mean that the battery is failing. Do not charge it, do not carry it in a pocket and do not try to repair or open it. Move it to a hard surface away from anything flammable, and dispose of it properly; see [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/). If a device ever smokes or becomes very hot, move away from it and call emergency services if there is a fire risk.

## Pocket and bag habits
Keep devices separate from coins and keys, which can short the battery terminals or press the fire button. Use a case if possible, and carry spare batteries in a proper case rather than loose. Avoid carrying a device in a back pocket, where sitting on it can bend it. For travel, follow the rules in [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/).

## Replaceable batteries
Box mods that use removable cells need correctly rated batteries from a reputable source. Never mix brands, ages or charge levels in the same device. Use cells whose wraps are in good condition, and replace any with tears or exposed metal. Check that the battery's current rating suits the device, because a battery that cannot supply enough current can overheat. Charge cells in a proper external charger on a hard surface, and never leave them charging unattended.

## Charging habits
Charge before the device is completely empty when you can, and unplug once it is full. Lithium-ion batteries last longer if they are not regularly run to zero or kept at a full charge for days. A partial top-up is fine. If you will not use a device for a long time, store it partly charged in a cool, dry place. See [extending battery life](/blog/how-to-extend-vape-battery-life/).

### Disposables with rechargeable batteries
Many large-capacity disposables have USB-C ports. Charge them as you would any small device, and do not keep charging them after they stop working, which can be a sign that the liquid is finished but the battery still holds a charge.

## Signs a battery is nearing the end
- The device runs out of charge much faster than it used to.
- It takes much longer to charge, or does not reach full.
- The casing feels warm even when idle.
- The device turns off by itself.
- There is any swelling, odor or leaking.

If you see any of these, retire the device. A new one costs far less than the risk.

## What to do in an emergency
If a battery starts to smoke or burn, do not touch it with bare hands. If you can do so without risk, move away from flammable items and call emergency services. Do not use water on a lithium battery fire unless instructed by emergency services; keep people and pets away. Afterward, do not use the device, and dispose of it as hazardous waste.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is it a problem to charge overnight?
It is better not to. If you do, use a hard, flat, non-flammable surface, a quality charger and a device in good condition, and never charge a damaged device.

### Can I use a phone charger?
Usually yes, if it is a reputable USB charger and the device uses a standard cable. Avoid very high-power fast chargers unless the manufacturer says they are supported.

### Why does my device get warm?
Slight warmth during charging or heavy use is normal. Hot to touch is not, and you should stop using it.

### How long do batteries last?
It depends on the device and how you use it. A battery that is looked after lasts longer, but eventually every battery wears out.

### Can I recycle a battery myself?
Take devices and batteries to a hazardous waste or electronics recycling site. Do not put them in household trash or curbside recycling.

## Where to shop
Browse [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/) and [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). Read the instructions that come with your device. All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A weekly habit check
Once a week, look at your device. Check the casing for dents, swelling or cracks. Check the charging port for bent pins or debris. Check the cable for fraying. Check that the device is not unusually warm when idle. Wipe the outside with a dry cloth. It takes a minute, and it catches problems before they become serious. If you carry spare batteries, check the wraps and the case at the same time.

## What to do with an old device
When a device reaches the end of its life, stop using it and take it for recycling instead of leaving it in a drawer. An old battery that is left unattended can degrade further. Follow the guidance in [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/). If you are replacing a device, choose one with a reputable battery and a standard charging port, and read the manufacturer's instructions before first use.

## Myths about batteries
- **"You must drain a battery before charging."** Modern lithium-ion batteries do not need it, and frequent full drains can shorten their life.
- **"Any charger is fine."** Poor chargers can damage batteries and are a common cause of problems.
- **"A warm battery is normal."** Slight warmth is normal. Hot to touch is not.
- **"A swollen battery is still usable."** It is not. Stop using it at once.

Knowing the facts helps you keep your devices working and reduces the chance of an incident.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is it normal for a disposable to stop working before the liquid is gone?
It can happen. Heavy use, heat and cold all reduce battery life, and a non-rechargeable device may stop when the battery is spent. Do not try to open it. Take it for recycling.

### Can I use a vape while it is charging?
It is better not to. Using a device while it charges makes it hotter, and some devices are not designed for it. Unplug it, then use it.

### Should I keep spare batteries in the fridge?
No. Store them at room temperature in a case, away from heat and moisture.

### What if I drop my device?
Check it for dents and cracks. If it is damaged, or if it feels warm or smells odd afterward, stop using it and dispose of it properly.
